limitations: Docker Hub and Chocolatey listings reflect a snapshot search on 2026-09-22 and community package freshness/maintenance can change without notice.

Sub-scores are an explicit, declared linear rubric (5 x 20-point checks) rather than a continuous market-share measurement; they are intended to be reproducible and applied identically to every language, not to imply false numeric precision.

caveats: Kotlin requires a JDK as a prerequisite for the CLI/compiler path, which is an extra dependency compared to fully self-contained native toolchains; this is reflected qualitatively but not double-counted as a separate sub-check.
Windows CLI installation is comparatively more manual: official docs recommend manual install on Windows versus SDKMAN on UNIX-like systems.
metric.installation_distribution_experie.rubric: Frozen 5-part rubric, 20 pts each, applied identically to every language from the same evidence-collection depth (official docs + package-index/registry pages, one retrieval pass per sub-check): (1) official cross-platform standalone binary distribution (Win/macOS/Linux) via the project's own release channel; (2) first-class support in a widely used version manager documented by the project itself; (3) availability through general-purpose OS/system package managers (official or well-maintained community); (4) zero-friction bundled path where a mainstream IDE ships the toolchain out of the box; (5) container/CI-friendly distribution and build-tool auto-provisioning that avoids a manual install for typical project use.

citations: Kotlin docker images built upon official openjdk images.
An unofficial Docker image for running Kotlin scripts
container_ci_and_build_tool_autoprovisio.note: No official first-party Kotlin Docker image was found on Docker Hub; available images are community-built on top of official OpenJDK images. Typical Gradle/Maven-based projects avoid a manual install entirely because the build tool resolves the Kotlin toolchain automatically, which offsets some of the container-image gap.

citations: Download the latest version (kotlin-compiler-2.4.20.zip) from GitHub Releases.
Unzip the standalone compiler into a directory and optionally add the kotlinc/bin directory to the system path.
The bin directory contains the scripts needed to compile and run Kotlin on Windows, macOS, and Linux.
cross_platform_official_binaries.note: Official GitHub Releases ship a standalone compiler zip usable on Windows, macOS, and Linux.

citations: Installing the command-line compiler is not an essential step to use Kotlin.
The common approach is to write Kotlin applications using IDEs or code editors with official Kotlin support, such as IntelliJ IDEA or Android Studio.
They provide full Kotlin support right out of the box.
ide_bundled_zero_friction_path.note: Kotlin documentation itself frames IDE use (IntelliJ IDEA / Android Studio, both of which bundle the Kotlin plugin and compiler) as the common approach, with a standalone CLI compiler being optional.

citations: The command-line compiler can be installed via Homebrew, SDKMAN!, and MacPorts.
Ubuntu does not package sdkman for APT, and the visible Snap wrapper is unofficial, so the main path stays on the upstream Bash installer
system_package_manager_availability.note: Multiple mainstream package managers carry Kotlin (Homebrew, MacPorts, Chocolatey on Windows), though some of these (e.g. the Chocolatey package) are community-maintained rather than JetBrains-published, and Linux distro-native packaging (apt) is not first-party.

citations: An easier way to install Kotlin on UNIX-based systems, such as macOS, Linux, Cygwin, FreeBSD, and Solaris, is SDKMAN!.
Install Software Development Kits for the JVM such as Java, Scala, Kotlin and Groovy.
version_manager_support.note: Kotlin's own documentation names SDKMAN! as the recommended installation route on UNIX-like systems, and SDKMAN explicitly lists Kotlin as a first-class managed SDK alongside Java/Gradle/Maven.

metric.toolchain_stability_release_matur.rubric: Frozen 5-part rubric, 20 pts each, scored from currently observable, frozen evidence only (no credit or penalty for language age): (1) documented, predictable release cadence with defined release types; (2) documented versioning/support policy stating which versions receive fixes and for how long; (3) explicit compatibility guarantees (source/binary) with a defined deprecation/migration process; (4) a formal stability classification system applied to language/library components in the current stable release; (5) a multi-year continuous history of supported-artifact production without gaps, evidenced by the current release line.

citations: All binaries are backwards compatible; that means a newer compiler can read older binaries (for example, 1.3 understands 1.0 through 1.2).
A documented deprecation cycle replaces silent breaking changes, so anything we remove is announced, and developers are given time to adapt.
The Language Committee is the formal body that approves significant changes to the language.
Forward compatibility is not guaranteed.
For example, the 2.0.x compiler is not guaranteed to read binaries produced by the 2.1.x compiler.
compatibility_guarantees.note: Kotlin has a strong, formally documented backward-compatibility commitment for stable binaries and language features since 1.0, with a Language Committee governing changes and a documented deprecation cycle; the score is not a full 20 because forward compatibility is explicitly not guaranteed (a newer compiler can read older binaries, but not vice versa) and some cross-version guarantees are qualified (e.g., klib binaries only backward compatible from 1.9.20 onward).

citations: In May 2024, JetBrains released Kotlin 2.0 at KotlinConf 2024 as the most significant release in the language's history.
Starting with Kotlin 2.0.0, a new release policy was introduced with language releases every 6 months, tooling releases every 3 months, and bug fix releases as needed.
continuous_supported_artifact_history.note: Kotlin has shipped stable releases continuously since 1.0 (2016) through the current 2.x line (2.4.20 as of this snapshot), including a major compiler rewrite (K2) that preserved the release cadence and compatibility guarantees, indicating no gaps in supported-artifact production.

citations: Language releases (2. x. 0) that bring major changes in the language and include tooling updates.
Released once in 6 months.
Tooling releases (2. x. 20) that are shipped between language releases and include updates in the tooling, performance improvements, and bug fixes.
Released in 3 months after corresponding language release.
documented_release_cadence.note: Kotlin publishes a formal, date-driven release process with three defined release types and fixed intervals: language releases every 6 months, tooling releases 3 months after each language release, and bug-fix releases as needed.

citations: Stable means "use it even in most conservative scenarios": It's done.
We will be evolving it according to our strict backward compatibility rules.
We collectively refer to Experimental, Alpha and Beta as pre-stable levels.

A stable component may have an experimental subcomponent, for example: a stable compiler may have an experimental feature; a stable API may include experimental classes or functions; a stable command-line tool may have experimental options.
formal_stability_classification.note: Kotlin publishes an explicit, project-wide stability taxonomy (Experimental, Alpha, Beta, Stable) with precise meaning for each level, applied consistently to compiler features, platforms, and libraries, and each release's changelog explicitly lists which features graduated between levels.

citations: Starting with Kotlin 2.4, the Kotlin standard library now includes an 18-month security support policy, with security fixes backported across active release lines.
Support page (current supported lines, end-of-support dates, latest patches): kotl.in/stdlib-security · Security policy: kotlinlang.org/docs/security.html
versioning_support_policy.note: Kotlin documents API-version support depth (multiple prior API versions remain supported for compatibility) and, as of 2026, added an explicit standard-library security support policy with a published support page listing supported lines and end-of-support dates.

evidence.selection_and_sampling_method: For both metrics, evidence was drawn from JetBrains' own kotlinlang.org documentation (release process, evolution principles, component stability, command-line install page, security policy blog), supplemented by widely used third-party installation/package-manager references (SDKMAN.io, Homebrew/MacPorts mentions, Chocolatey and Docker Hub package listings) to check independent packaging channels. This is a fixed, declared set of route types (official docs + version manager site + OS package registries + container registry) applied at the same examination depth used for other languages in this shard family; no single popularity count (stars/downloads) was used as a standalone proxy.
